content: Poppy tea is a narcotic analgesic beverage brewed from the dried parts of the Papaver somniferum plant. It has been consumed for its psychoactive effects for as long as the poppy plant has been cultivated. Historical references to its use can be found in both Asian and Western literature, including depictions of opium dens. In some regions, the preparation of poppy tea is preferred over opium due to legal restrictions on the plant's latex, which is the primary component of opium. For example, in the Netherlands, all parts of the Papaver somniferum plant, except for the seeds, are classified as List I drugs under the Opium Law and are therefore illegal. However, due to its use for decorative purposes, the trade and possession of dried Papaver somniferum are not actively prosecuted unless there is intent for drug use, which is rarely enforced. This makes dried poppy material an alternative to pharmaceutical opioids, which are highly regulated in the Netherlands, as it is easily obtainable for decorative purposes. In the United States, it is legal to purchase poppy seeds, dried pods, and, in some cases, to grow the Papaver somniferum variety of poppies. However, using legally purchased items, such as seeds, to extract or concentrate opioids is illegal. Poppy tea contains two main groups of alkaloids: phenanthrenes (including morphine and codeine) and benzylisoquinolines (including papaverine). Morphine is the most prevalent alkaloid, comprising 8–14% of the total alkaloid content. The effects of poppy tea are primarily due to morphine binding to and activating mu-opioid receptors in the brain, spinal cord, stomach, and intestines. Preparation and Consumption Poppy tea can be prepared using either the seed pods or the seeds themselves. Dried poppy pods are typically crushed into a fine, straw-like substance to facilitate efficient extraction. This material, known as poppy straw, is steeped in hot water that has been slightly acidified with vinegar or citric acid. After steeping for a few minutes, the mixture is strained, and the resulting brown liquid is consumed. The effects of the tea begin approximately 30 minutes after ingestion and can last up to 8 hours. The tea is intensely bitter, and users often add flavorings to improve its taste. Grapefruit juice is sometimes added, as it may inhibit liver enzyme activity, thereby increasing the strength and duration of the opiate effects. Some users evaporate the tea over low heat to create a concentrated liquid or dry powder, which can then be encapsulated for more precise dosing. While oral consumption is the most common method, dried poppy tea can also be snorted or smoked. However, these methods often result in unpleasant side effects due to the presence of non-active and potentially irritating substances. It is important to note that dried poppy tea is distinct from opium, as the former is made from the whole plant, while the latter is derived solely from the exuded latex. Green (undried) poppy pods can also be used to make tea, although dried pods are often preferred for large-scale production of pure opium due to their ease of grinding into a fine powder. To prepare tea from green pods, the pods are blended into a fine mash, which is then heated with water over medium heat. The mixture should not be allowed to boil, as this may destroy the active alkaloids. The heated mash is then mixed with lemon and honey and steeped for 15 minutes before consumption. Effects The effects of poppy tea vary widely depending on factors such as dosage, the alkaloid content of the poppies, the quality of the extraction, individual sensitivity, and any pre-existing opiate tolerance. The tea contains the base compounds from which all natural, semi-synthetic, and synthetic opiates are derived. Users typically experience a warming sensation of the skin and body during the onset of effects. Due to the presence of opioid receptors in the spinal cord and digestive tract, users often report sensations of lightness and pleasure in the intestinal tract. This is followed by an elevated mood, extreme euphoria, and a sense of well-being. Physical signs include constricted pupils, flushing of the face, neck, and extremities, and itching due to histamine release as the liver metabolizes the alkaloids. Side Effects and Tolerance Side effects increase with dosage and may include drowsiness, mild stomachache, lethargy, itching, slowed breathing, and nausea. Nausea is often attributed to the presence of noscapine and is more common in first-time or inexperienced users. At high doses, the side effects can become dangerous and may result in death due to respiratory depression or choking on vomit. Regular use of poppy tea leads to tolerance and dependence, with chemical dependency developing after one to two weeks of daily use. Abrupt cessation following frequent use can result in withdrawal symptoms, including leg and abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, insomnia, cravings, and anxiety. While physical withdrawal symptoms typically subside within 4–10 days, psychological dependence and cravings may persist for a longer period. Overdose Overdosing on poppy tea is relatively easy, as the recreational dose is not significantly lower than the dose at which side effects become unpleasant or dangerous. Experienced users often start with a modest initial dose and gradually increase it over time to reach the desired effect. A fatal overdose case was reported in 2003, where an individual consumed tea made from 5 pounds of poppy seeds. Laboratory analysis revealed a morphine concentration of approximately 250 μg/mL in the tea, with the individual having consumed around 500 mg of morphine—about five times the lethal oral dose for someone without opiate tolerance. This incident was reported by ABC News in January 2008.
